source.title: Optimization Matters: Guidelines to Improve Representation Learning with Deep Networks

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; some table and figure layout is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies optimizers and batch sizes and measures held-out feature-classification accuracy, a different measure from the train–test generalization gap in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports test accuracy of SVMs trained on learned CNN features. It does not report random-label fitting, train–test gaps, or the measured network properties in V1–V3 and V6–V8.
record.test_reason: The study compares optimizers using held-out accuracy of linear SVMs on learned CNN features, bearing on V4 through a different evaluation method. ResNet50 batch comparisons also test V5: training lasts 50 epochs from scratch and 25 epochs from pretrained weights, with batch size varied within each initialization group. Neither version requires a measured train–test gap.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that learning rate, batch size, initialization, and scheduling affect representation quality; appropriate choices improve results and defaults can be suboptimal. They find no single best optimizer and suggest adaptive advantages in transfer learning and fine-grained tasks. Their general recommendation for decay has exceptions in the tables.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates learned feature spaces using a linear SVM on the original dataset train/test splits; it does not use the claim versions' train–test-gap, random-label, or sharpness measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, initialization (random or pretrained), learning-rate schedule, and architecture affect the reported feature-classification accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Learning-rate schedules and initialization alter feature quality; within-optimizer schedule improvements alone do not establish V4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The discriminative quality of CNN representations depends on learning-rate schedule and initialization.

record.peer_reviewed: Anais do XVIII Encontro Nacional de Inteligência Artificial e Computacional (ENIAC 2021)
record.problems: The paper evaluates test accuracy of an SVM on learned features rather than reporting network training and test errors or their gap. It does not report random-label controls. The initial CNN's epoch budget is not stated in the supplied text; later experiments use different epoch counts. Several conclusions are qualitative summaries of extensive tables.
record.rows_left_out: The tables report many optimizer × learning-rate × batch-size × initialization combinations. Individual cells are not separately extracted because the relevant claim versions concern generalization gaps and fixed-epoch batch comparisons, neither of which is directly measured; the table summaries and outcome-changing conditions are represented in R1–R5.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Direct CNN prediction accuracy; matched training-performance comparisons; language benchmarks; broader optimizer-specific tuning; decoupled weight decay; switching optimizers.
Explicit fixed-epoch comparisons for the initial CNN and MobileNetV2; language models; longer training, learning-rate scaling with warmup, and normalization or regularization interventions.
Dropout interventions. ResNet50 uses dropout, but there is no comparison removing or varying it.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Existing rows aggregate incompatible conditions and need splitting before assigning single states. Detailed table cells are already declared omitted in rows_left_out. Unreported epoch budgets are an evidential limitation, not a demonstrated limit on V5.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Network-width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.

Image-classification and language benchmarks beyond the studied datasets and feature-SVM evaluation; training-performance comparisons; broader tuning; decoupled weight decay; switching from Adam to SGD; word-level language models.
Fixed-epoch-budget comparisons and language models; whether longer training, warmup, normalization, or regularization changes remove a large-batch penalty.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to generalization gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: smaller CNN architecture
rows.operation_detail: Train with SGD, Adam, or RAdam across learning rates and batch sizes; evaluate SVM classification accuracy on learned features.
rows.measure: SVM classification accuracy (%) on learned features; the text reports that all methods achieved approximately 92% with suitable configurations, and that Adam/RAdam performed well with smaller learning rates and larger batches.
rows.value: Approximately 92% accuracy across methods with suitable configurations; Adam/RAdam may improve results with smaller learning rates and batches up to 512.
rows.uncertainty: Table 1 reports values with ± quantities; this summary statement gives no uncertainty.
rows.note: The paper describes held-out feature classification, not a train–test gap or matched training performance. The summary is retained as reported rather than reconstructing a single optimizer's table value.
rows.check: At the stated learning rate 0.001 and batches 128–512, Adam/RAdam outperform SGD: adaptive accuracy is 91.4–91.9%, versus SGD's 78.2%, 60.2%, and 35.8%. The approximately equal best accuracies concern different learning rates and batches, so they require a separate condition group. The initial CNN's epoch budget is unspecified, preventing a V5 verdict.

source_check.correct: At learning rate 0.001 and batches 128, 256, 512, SGD accuracies are 78.2%, 60.2%, 35.8%; Adam accuracies are 91.4%, 91.8%, 91.9%; RAdam accuracies are 91.7%, 91.5%, 91.7%. Approximately equal best accuracies across optimizers require separately selected configurations, including higher learning rates for SGD.
source_check.problem: The approximately 92% summary across methods does not apply to SGD under the row's listed settings.

rows.subject: smaller CNN architecture
rows.operation_detail: Train with SGD, Adam, or RAdam across learning rates and batch sizes; evaluate SVM classification accuracy on learned features.
rows.measure: SVM classification accuracy (%) on learned features; the text says Adam/RAdam were overall better than SGD, with smaller learning rates and large batches preferable.
rows.value: Adam/RAdam were overall better than SGD; smaller learning rates and large batches were preferable.
rows.uncertainty: Table 2 reports values with ± quantities; this summary statement gives no uncertainty.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison. It does not establish a fixed-epoch large-batch penalty or compare training performance.
rows.check: At learning rate 0.001 and batches 128–512, adaptive accuracy is 63.3–64.4%, versus SGD's 30.1%, 21.3%, and 15.7%. Across the full search, adaptive maxima are also slightly higher than SGD's 63%. The initial CNN's epoch budget is unspecified, preventing a V5 verdict.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch and fine-tuned from ImageNet-pretrained weights
rows.operation_detail: Train with SGD or RAdam at varying learning rates and batch sizes; evaluate SVM classification accuracy on learned features.
rows.measure: SVM classification accuracy (%) on learned features.
rows.value: From scratch, results reach up to 84% after 50 epochs; from pretrained weights, approximately 82% is achieved after 25 epochs. The text says extreme choices affect SGD less, and appropriate choices yield similar accuracies.
rows.uncertainty: Tables 3 reports ± quantities; summary values give no uncertainty.
rows.note: The reported summary does not isolate batch size effects from learning rate, optimizer, and initialization.
rows.check: Split by optimizer, learning rate, initialization, and comparison. One partial state cannot represent these mixed results. Table 3 gives best scratch accuracies of 84.6% for SGD and 84.4% for RAdam, and pretrained maxima of 81.4% and 82.3%. Within each initialization, epochs are fixed across batches. Most settings lose accuracy with larger batches, but scratch RAdam at learning rate 0.01 improves from 57.3% at batch 32 to 72.2% at batch 256. The prose's reference to RAdam learning rate 0.1 conflicts with the table's 0.01.

source_check.problem: The aggregate summary cannot express the different optimizer and batch effects; the condition-specific verdicts require Table 3 comparisons.

rows.subject: MobileNetV2
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch and fine-tuned from ImageNet-pretrained weights
rows.operation_detail: Train with SGD or RAdam at varying learning rates and batch sizes; evaluate SVM classification accuracy on learned features.
rows.measure: SVM classification accuracy (%) on learned features.
rows.value: SGD favors lower learning rates on Flowers; the paper says its general behavior is not repeated for this fine-grained dataset.
rows.uncertainty: Table 5 reports ± quantities; the text summary gives no uncertainty.
rows.note: This is a dataset-specific optimizer/learning-rate qualification; the summary does not identify a batch-size effect.
rows.check: The row reports a learning-rate preference without the optimizer comparison. Table 5 shows scratch maxima of 80.5% for SGD and 90.1% for RAdam, and pretrained maxima of 94.7% and 96%. These favor RAdam. MobileNetV2's epoch budget is not explicitly given, so its batch results cannot establish V5's fixed-budget condition.

source_check.problem: The learning-rate summary alone does not establish reversal of V4; Table 5 supplies the supporting optimizer comparisons.

rows.subject: MobileNetV2
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch and fine-tuned from ImageNet-pretrained weights
rows.operation_detail: Compare step and exponential learning-rate decay at fixed batch size.
rows.measure: SVM classification accuracy (%) on learned features.
rows.baseline: Step Decay or Exponential Decay, depending on the paired comparison.
rows.value: The text says exponential decay is slightly higher for SGD; for RAdam, exponential decay is better with random weights and Step Decay stands out with pretrained weights, reaching approximately 97% on Flowers with initial learning rate 0.0001.
rows.uncertainty: Table 6 reports ± quantities; the summary gives no uncertainty for its approximate value.
rows.note: The paper identifies schedule and initialization as conditions that change the comparison; it does not report training accuracy alongside test accuracy.
rows.check: Schedule improvements within an optimizer do not themselves establish an adaptive-versus-SGD ranking. Split into paired optimizer comparisons. With scratch CIFAR-10 features, RAdam exceeds SGD under both schedules; pretrained results also favor RAdam. Flowers rankings depend on initialization and schedule. The claimed general scheduling improvement has exceptions in Table 6.
